title: Stratford-upon-Avon
subtitle: Shakespeare's life, walked in order
intro: Shakespeare's whole life, walked in order through the town where it happened: a family in trouble, a schoolboy, a marriage at 18, a rise in London, a servant of the king, and a legend.

dayGlance.title: His youth
dayGlance.sub: The Birthplace, his school and Anne Hathaway's Cottage.

dayGlance.title: The legend
dayGlance.sub: The theatre, the statue and the river.

actsLede: Six parts, in the order he lived them.

acts.label: Act 1 · 1564: born into trouble
acts.tagline: A family that climbed, then fell.
acts.narrative: His father married into a landowning family, rose to run the town, then was taken to court and fell into debt.

acts.label: Act 2 · The schoolboy
acts.tagline: A free school, and the first actors in town.
acts.narrative: Latin six days a week, and the first touring actors performing in the hall downstairs.

acts.label: Act 3 · Married at 18
acts.tagline: A wife, three children, then gone.
acts.narrative: He married an older, pregnant farmer's daughter, had three children by 20, and left for London.

acts.label: Act 4 · The rise
acts.narrative: Mocked as an upstart, he wrote for a rich patron in the plague years, then became an owner of his company and of the Globe.

acts.label: Act 5 · The king's man, and the end
acts.tagline: Royal servant, rich man, a grave he paid for.
acts.narrative: The king took over his company. He invested at home, protected his daughter in his will, and paid for his own grave.

acts.label: Act 6 · The legend
acts.tagline: The family ended. The name didn't.
acts.narrative: His friends saved his plays, a rained-out festival made Stratford famous, and his birthplace was nearly shipped to America.

The Birthplace has timed entry, so book ahead. To do it all in one day, start at the Birthplace at 10: New Place has the shortest hours (11 to 3 in autumn), and the church is only open on Sunday afternoons. Hall's Croft and Mary Arden's Farm are closed to visitors. Coming twice instead? Split after Anne Hathaway's Cottage: his youth on the first visit, then the rise, the end and the legend on the second.

birthplace.name: Shakespeare's Birthplace
birthplace.onCamera: This is where it all starts. William Shakespeare was born in this house in 1564. Today he's probably the most famous writer in the world. But he didn't start out important. His family was ordinary, and when he was a boy they got into serious trouble. I think that explains everything he did later.
facts: The first record of his family is right here. In 1552 his father was fined for leaving a pile of rubbish and dung in this street.

His father, John, made gloves. His wife, Mary Arden, came from a farming family that owned land. In fact, John's own father rented his farm from Mary's father. John kept climbing: he bought houses, joined the town council, and in 1568 he got the top job in town, like a mayor.

Then it went wrong. He was taken to court for trading wool without a licence, and for lending money at illegal interest. He got into debt, stopped going to council meetings, and his request for a family coat of arms went nowhere. William was about 12.
birthplace.closeOnCamera: So that's the boy. A family that had climbed up, then fallen. Everything he did later, the money, the houses, the coat of arms, was about climbing back. And it started at school, five minutes down the road.

routeCard.note: Enter through the Shakespeare Centre on Henley Street.

see: The room where he was born
The old timber fronts of Henley Street
planCard.todo: Timed entry, so book ahead. Open 10 to 5 from spring to autumn. Your ticket also covers New Place. Then walk to the school, about 6 minutes.

schoolroom.name: Shakespeare's Schoolroom and Guildhall
schoolroom.onCamera: This is almost certainly where Shakespeare went to school. Think about that. The boy who went on to write Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Macbeth sat his lessons in this room. And the hall downstairs has its own part in his story.
facts: It was a free school for boys from the town. Lessons were in Latin, from early morning to late afternoon, Monday to Saturday. Nobody can prove he came here, but it was free, it was five minutes from his house, and his father was one of the town's leaders.

The first time travelling actors are recorded performing in Stratford was in 1568, in the hall downstairs. That year his father had the top job in town, so he would have been in the audience. William was four.
schoolroom.closeOnCamera: He never went to university. That's why some people still say a nobleman must have written his plays. And remember it, because in London it will be thrown back at him. But first, at 18, he married a farmer's daughter from Shottery, a village a mile away. Let's walk there.

routeCard.note: The schoolroom is upstairs. The Guildhall, the medieval town hall, is downstairs.

see: On the way: Harvard House on High Street (1596), the family home of John Harvard's mother. Harvard University is named after him.
Timber houses from the 1400s next door, built for poor old people
planCard.todo: Open 11 to 5, last entry 4:15. £10 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket, £15 on its own. Then walk to Anne Hathaway's Cottage in Shottery, about 25 minutes.

anne-hathaway.name: Anne Hathaway's Cottage
anne-hathaway.onCamera: This is where Anne Hathaway grew up. In 1582, an 18-year-old William Shakespeare married her. She was eight years older than him, and she was already pregnant. It was one of the biggest decisions of his life, and it shaped everything that came next.
facts: In Shakespeare's day this was Hewlands Farm, with more than 90 acres. Anne's family farmed here for generations. Her father had died the year before the wedding.
Their daughter Susanna was born six months after the wedding. Two years later came twins, Hamnet and Judith. By 20, William had a wife and three children.
anne-hathaway.closeOnCamera: Then, at some point, he left. Anne and the children stayed in Stratford, and William went to London. For about seven years after the twins were born, nobody knows exactly where he was. Historians call them the lost years. When he appears again, he's in London, and he's about to get rich.

routeCard.sub: Cottage Lane, Shottery · a mile from the centre
routeCard.note: About 25 minutes on foot from the school.

planCard.todo: Open 10 to 5. £5 if you add it to your Birthplace ticket. Then walk back into the centre to New Place, about 25 minutes.

new-place.name: Shakespeare's New Place
new-place.onCamera: This is where Shakespeare lived when he was rich. He bought a house on this spot in 1597, when he was 33. It was one of the biggest houses in his home town. Five years earlier, in London, people were laughing at him. So how does a glove-maker's son pull that off? Here's how.
facts: His first appearance in London is an insult. In 1592 a pamphlet by a jealous rival called him an 'upstart crow': a common actor, with no university education, who thought he could write as well as his betters.

Then plague closed London's theatres for more than a year. So he wrote long poems for a rich young nobleman, the Earl of Southampton. One of them, Venus and Adonis, was the biggest bestseller of his whole life.

When the theatres reopened in 1594, he made the smartest move of his career. He didn't just write for an acting company. He became one of its owners. They performed for Queen Elizabeth the First, and now he got a share of the profits, not just a writer's fee.

In 1598 their landlord refused to renew the lease on their theatre. So, while he was away for Christmas, the company took the whole building apart, carried the timber across the River Thames, and built the Globe Theatre with it. Shakespeare owned part of the Globe.
new-place.closeOnCamera: And the money came home. In 1596 he finally got his father that coat of arms, making the family gentlemen. That same year his only son, Hamnet, died. He was 11. The next year Shakespeare bought the house that stood right here. It's gone now: in 1759 its owner, a priest tired of tourists and fighting the town over tax, knocked it down.

routeCard.note: Enter by the gate on Chapel Street.

see: The garden where the house stood
Nash's House next door: the home of Thomas Nash, who married Shakespeare's granddaughter Elizabeth
planCard.todo: Included in your Birthplace ticket. Check the hours: in autumn it's open 11 to 3. Then walk to Holy Trinity, about 7 minutes.

holy-trinity.name: Holy Trinity Church
holy-trinity.angle: 1603–1616 · The king's man, and the end
holy-trinity.onCamera: By the end of his life, Shakespeare wasn't just a successful writer. He worked for the king, he owned land and houses, and he was one of the richest men in his home town. He came back to Stratford for his last years, and died in 1616, aged 52. This is his grave. And even this spot, he paid for.
facts: In 1603 the new king, James the First, took over Shakespeare's company. They became the King's Men, the king's own actors. Shakespeare was named second in the list, and he was given red royal cloth to wear as a servant of the king.

He kept investing at home. In 1605 he paid £440, a fortune at the time, for a share of the church's income. That's what gave him the right to be buried in here, next to the altar, instead of outside in the churchyard.

A month before he died, he rewrote his will. His daughter Judith had just married a man who was then caught in a scandal, so Shakespeare protected her money from him. His wife Anne got just one thing by name: his 'second-best bed'.
holy-trinity.closeOnCamera: Now look at the stone: 'Cursed be he that moves my bones.' In 2016 a radar scan found the head end disturbed, which fits an old story that his skull was stolen. The church isn't convinced. And here's the sad part. He spent his life building a family name. But his last grandchild died in 1670, with no children. The family ended. The name didn't.

routeCard.note: Go in by the avenue of lime trees.

see: On the way: Hall's Croft, where his daughter Susanna lived with her husband, Dr John Hall. They married in this church in 1607.
planCard.todo: Hours change with the day and the season, and on Sundays it's only open in the afternoon. The grave costs £5. It's a working church, so keep your voice down. Then walk along the river to the theatre, about 8 minutes.

theatre.name: The Royal Shakespeare Theatre
theatre.angle: After 1616 · How he became a legend
theatre.onCamera: When Shakespeare died, he was famous in London. But he wasn't a legend yet. That took a book, a festival that went badly wrong, and a rumour about an American showman. And a lot of it happened right here, in this town.
facts: Seven years after he died, two actors from his company printed his plays in one big book, the First Folio. Eighteen of the plays had never been printed before, including Macbeth and The Tempest. Without that book, we'd probably have lost them.

In September 1769, the most famous actor of the day, David Garrick, threw a three-day festival here for Shakespeare. It poured with rain, the river rose, and not a single Shakespeare play was performed. But it worked. After that, people started coming to Stratford to see where Shakespeare lived.

In 1847 his birthplace, the house where we started this walk, was put up for sale. Newspapers claimed the American showman P. T. Barnum wanted to buy it and ship it to America. Historians doubt he ever really tried, but people panicked. Charles Dickens helped raise £3,000, and the house was bought and saved.
theatre.closeOnCamera: And this theatre opened on 23 April 1932, the day Stratford celebrates his birthday. It was designed by Elisabeth Scott. She was 29, and the only woman out of 70 architects in the competition. Now, one last stop: his statue.

planCard.todo: Then walk on to the statue in Bancroft Gardens, about 3 minutes.

river.name: The statue, the garden and the bridge
river.onCamera: Shakespeare died 400 years ago. But you've probably quoted him without knowing it. His words are in the way we talk, his plays shaped how England sees its own history, and this whole town still lives off his name. So what did he actually leave behind?
facts: 'Green-eyed monster.' 'A wild-goose chase.' 'It's all Greek to me.' All of these reached everyday English through his plays. People say he invented 1,700 words. That's an exaggeration, but hundreds of words and phrases came to us through him.

He also shaped how England sees its own past. He made King Richard the Third into a famous villain, while writing for Queen Elizabeth the First, whose grandfather had taken Richard's crown. And in 1944, during the Second World War, the British government paid for a film of his play Henry the Fifth, about an English king who invades France and wins. It was made to lift spirits around D-Day.
river.closeOnCamera: A glove-maker's son from a small country town. Laughed at in London, rich as an owner, a servant of the king. And 400 years later: a theatre, a statue, and the words we speak.

The narrowboats in the canal basin

coldOpen.title: Cold open
facts: Everyone knows this man as a poet. But there's another story about him that I'd like to tell you. Today I'm walking through his whole life, in order, in the town where it all happened. A family that lost everything. A young man laughed at as an upstart. A theatre taken apart behind the landlord's back. And a grave with a curse on it.

signOff.title: Closing sign-off
facts: So that's his life, from the house where he was born to this statue by the river. A family that fell, a schoolboy, a husband at 18, a man who got rich by owning instead of writing, a servant of the king, and a grave he paid for. His family line ended. His words didn't. If you enjoyed this, like and subscribe, and tell me where I should go next.
